board.evidence_status: Public research through 2026-09-12. Future actions and outcomes are a model simulation. No actual pilot store or customer records are supplied.
board.measurement_rule: Null means unmeasured. Keep real measurement fields null and complete observed sample counts at zero without sourced operating records. Put hypothetical estimates in separately named simulated_* fields with assumptions, never in observed fields. Maintain a concise public_strategy_history of observable implemented actions and consequences so later players can adapt. Do not publish private budgets, dossiers or unseen internal intentions. Advance calendar_period to the end of the current month.
board.public_market_context: Starbucks is investing in coffeehouse service, staffing and Smart Queue while US transactions are growing. Dutch Bros offers drive-through beverages and Order Ahead at participating shops. Dunkin offers coffee-and-food value and mobile ordering through a franchise network. Some morning purchases can shift to home preparation or disappear. Local overlaps and customer segments in this exercise are assumptions.

decision.launch_period: January 2027; a proposed experiment, not an announced Starbucks policy
decision.offer: Capacity-aware mobile pickup slots with a protected café-order allocation from 7–10 a.m. on weekdays
decision.pricing: Keep beverage prices unchanged; assumed $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before added staffing, not a reported company figure
decision.scope: 50 pilot cafés and 50 comparison cafés; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders at peak; no automatic transfer of the policy to other stores
decision.segment: 50 US company-operated cafés with nearby Dutch Bros and Dunkin alternatives, paired with 50 comparison cafés
decision.statement: Pilot peak-time mobile-order admission limits in 50 US Starbucks cafés during January–March 2027, reserving 20% of measured production capacity for café orders and offering later pickup slots when the mobile allocation is full.

capabilities: Use existing sequencing and staffing practices as the implementation base (h4).
Offer honest later pickup times, test narrower reservation windows and release unused capacity within the pilot (h5).
Build paired-store measurement, attempt-to-purchase funnels and baseline cohorts using internal instrumentation (h8, h9).
constraints: The two-hour staff allowance, unchanged prices and 50-store limit are binding game constraints (h5).
Segment margin is not a local cost curve; no store p90 waits or mobile churn elasticity is known (h2, h6, h8).
A booked later slot is not revenue until a purchase completes; competitor substitution is only partly observable (h8).

facts.claim: Reported history: Starbucks began in Seattle in 1971. Its evolution from a bean merchant into a coffeehouse makes the in-store experience part of the proposition, not simply a distribution expense. The strategic implication is an author inference.

Reported financials: Q3 fiscal 2026 North America revenue was $7,395.1 million, operating income $1,008.9 million and operating margin 13.6%. These are segment figures, not pilot-store unit economics.
Reported demand: US comparable sales increased 7.9% and comparable transactions 4.2% in Q3 fiscal 2026. This case tests sustaining growth; it does not assume that current transactions are declining.

Reported strategy: Back to Starbucks combines staffing and scheduling investment, Smart Queue order sequencing, and restoration of the coffeehouse experience. These capabilities are public; the proposed 20% reservation is not an announced policy.

Assumed operating authority: 50 pilot and 50 comparison company-operated cafés; weekdays 07:00–10:00; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders. Price unchanged. Each pilot café may add at most two peak staff-hours per weekday. Rollback or narrower time windows are allowed; expansion beyond 50 is not.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed economics: $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before additional staffing. Assume fully loaded incremental labor costs $30/hour for sensitivity calculations. Two added hours cost $60/store/day and require 20 genuinely incremental transactions to break even before other costs. No actual store margins, baselines or demand elasticities are supplied.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed management problem: The operations lead is accountable for café service and labor spend; the digital lead for reliable pickup and repeat behavior; the finance lead for all-channel contribution. Optimizing one channel at another’s expense is not success. These are role tensions constructed for the game, not testimony from executives.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed information rights: The team can instrument its own order attempts, offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, staffing hours and baseline-linked repeat purchases; it cannot see rivals’ transaction logs or know where a rejected mobile user ultimately buys. Available instrumentation is a capability, not already collected evidence.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed decision rules: By round two seek at least a 20% adjusted café p90 wait reduction across 40 complete pairs. By round three require nonnegative daily contribution and no worse than a 3pp adjusted repeat decline with 1,000 complete customers per arm. Missing evidence cannot pass these gates.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

incentives: Restore a credible coffeehouse visit without sacrificing digital convenience (h1, h4).
Defend positive transaction momentum while earning back added labor through all-channel contribution (h2, h3, h6).
Make a reversible operational choice before the March decision deadline (h5, h9).
red_lines: Do not invent operating measurements or declare the economics gate passed from a better wait-time story alone (h6, h9).
Do not promise a national rollout or exceed the staffing cap (h5).

chain.claim: Starbucks implements capacity-aware mobile pickup slots in 50 pilot cafés during weekday peak, reserving 20% of measured 15-minute production capacity for in-café orders. Later mobile pickup times are offered when allocation is full. Up to two incremental staff hours per peak morning are permitted per pilot café.

Starbucks instruments all order attempts, offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, and incremental staffing hours in both pilot and 50 comparison cafés, beginning baseline and intervention measurement.

Commuters abandon Starbucks mobile orders if delayed at all, seeking a competitor on their direct route or skipping coffee. Habitual app users accept up to 8 minutes’ delay, but, if this happens more than twice a week or the delay is longer, they try Dunkin’ or Dutch Bros. Café visitors continue to order inside, expecting a better experience from the reserved capacity.

Dunkin launches a local opt-in $6 breakfast Meal Deal in 15 consenting franchise stores near pilot cafés for January 2027, promoted via the Dunkin app with advance ordering and rewards. Franchisees monitor basket contribution, repeat visits, and staffing costs, with stop rules to exit stores where the offer reduces profitability or cannibalizes full-price sales. Shared local marketing emphasizes value and convenience.

Dutch Bros launches a geo-fenced digital advertising campaign targeting areas around 12 shops during weekday peak hours, highlighting Order Ahead and offering a $1 credit for first-time Order Ahead users. Staffing is proactively adjusted for peak throughput. App and in-store messaging reinforce speed and convenience.

public_strategy_history: January 2027: Starbucks launches peak-hour mobile pickup slot limits and reserves 20% of capacity for in-café orders in 50 pilot cafés. Instrumentation begins for pilot and comparison cafés.

January 2027: Dunkin launches a $6 breakfast Meal Deal bundle in 15 consenting franchise stores near pilot cafés, with app promotion and local marketing. Store-level stop rules and monitoring are in place.
January 2027: Dutch Bros launches a geo-fenced digital campaign promoting Order Ahead and a $1 credit for first-time users in 12 shops, with peak-hour staffing adjustments and messaging.

January 2027: Morning customer segments respond: commuters abandon delayed Starbucks mobile orders, habitual app users tolerate limited delays but may switch after repeated issues, and café visitors continue in-person orders expecting improved experience.

outcome.description: All round-one actions are executed as described. Starbucks launches the capacity-aware mobile pickup pilot and begins instrumentation. Dunkin and Dutch Bros deploy their local offers and staffing adjustments. Customer segments respond according to their stated contingencies. No outcome metrics are yet observed.

pilot-jan27-integrated.rationale: All committed actions are within stated capabilities and constraints for the January 2027 period. Starbucks executes the pilot as described, limiting mobile pickup slots in 50 pilot cafés during peak hours and reserving 20% of capacity for in-café orders. Instrumentation and measurement begin as planned. Buyer segments respond as committed: commuters abandon delayed mobile orders and may switch or skip, habitual app users tolerate some delay but defect if reliability drops, and café visitors expect a less crowded in-store experience. Dunkin and Dutch Bros both launch targeted local offers and marketing campaigns, aiming to capture any displaced Starbucks demand, but remain within budget and operational constraints. No party exceeds its stated authority, budget, or scope. No kill criteria are met at this stage. No measured outcomes are available yet; this round sets the experimental and competitive context for future evaluation.
